title: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
desc: Promotes everyday experimentation and shared implementation while preserving reliability, access-to-justice and judicial-legitimacy concerns.

kps.k: The cluster advances a practitioner-led case for learning and redesigning legal work with AI, rather than waiting for technological certainty.
kps.d: Jen Leonard and Bridget McCormack frame AI as a general-purpose technology that could expand professional capacity, improve working lives and address unmet legal need. Their proposed response combines practical experimentation, continuing education and participation in governance. They argue that disengagement leaves technology companies to shape legal practice. This is principally an experience-based reform agenda, not evidence that adoption necessarily produces those benefits. Jason Tashea supplies a contrasting caution: present deployment should not rest on developers’ promises of future improvement.

qs.q: So we wanted to share what we've learned along the way—resources, our experiences working with generative AI, and an optimistic perspective about how this technology can transform legal services, legal education, and the practice of law for the better.

kps.k: Useful adoption depends on human implementation, relevant context and shared responsibility—not simply purchasing software or appointing a technology champion.
kps.d: Leonard identifies human buy-in as the central implementation challenge. At Quinn Emanuel, Jen Reeves favors practicing lawyers shaping workflows with innovation specialists’ support over rigid instructions imposed from outside daily practice. Nick Fleisher describes embedded former lawyers and legal-operations leaders, office hours and attention to inputs as Sandstone’s implementation approach. AAA’s experience similarly combines legal expertise, technical development and workflow mapping. These accounts support tailored, organization-wide learning, but provide no comparative evidence that one adoption model performs best. The hosts also identify resource and training disadvantages for courts and smaller practices.

kps.k: Everyday AI use provides a route into professional experimentation, but perceived convenience does not establish legal reliability.
kps.d: The hosts and guests describe AI as an available thinking partner for presentation preparation, research framing, drafting, learning and personal planning. Their proposed mechanism is iterative assistance: humans supply context, select useful suggestions and retain control over substance. Leonard’s workshop example explicitly rejects unsuitable ideas; Dave Hoffman reports collecting and comparing journal AI policies despite operational interruptions. Accounts of stale memory, sycophancy and context-entry difficulties qualify enthusiasm. These examples demonstrate reported use and satisfaction, not general accuracy, productivity or autonomous legal expertise.

kps.k: Access-to-justice arguments focus on making legal understanding and dispute resolution available where conventional representation does not reach.
kps.d: McCormack cites valid claims whose damages cannot attract lawyers and procedures that burden self-represented litigants. Leonard and Cat Moon advocate exploring direct public assistance and greater legal-aid capacity. Concrete illustrations remain limited: David Slayton reports faster navigation through LA Court’s deployed Court Help tool, while the hosts recount a tenant’s successful appeal through a second-hand AI-clinic story without establishing AI’s causal contribution. Moon’s reported twofold legal-aid adoption rate concerns uptake, not reduced unmet need. Cheaper participation also raises questions about agency comment processes and enterprise exposure, prompting recommendations for advance response planning rather than claims of demonstrated harm.

kps.k: The judicial-AI debate turns on both comparison with imperfect human systems and preservation of procedural legitimacy.
kps.d: McCormack asks whether AI should be compared with actual human judging and unavailable legal help, rather than an error-free ideal. Angela Tripp similarly proposes task-specific human-error comparisons as a way to build confidence. Zach Abramowitz calls differing support for lawyers’ and adjudicators’ AI use a double standard, citing nearly 90% versus 23%; however, the surveyed activities differ between research and analytics and decision-making. Against this comparative argument stand concerns about fabricated authorities, lost litigant voice and authentic evidence. McCormack retains a central role for respectful human explanation, invoking procedural-fairness literature without supplying individual studies. These arguments do not establish that AI improves judicial outcomes.

kps.k: Concrete initiatives favor bounded assistance and human accountability, even when their labels suggest autonomous legal services.

The LawNext account specifies human validation and final sign-off on awards, and McCormack separately confirms human oversight. Pennsylvania’s reported interim policy permits approved, low-risk judicial assistance with human review and confidentiality protections. Deployment, planned launch and oversight arrangements should remain distinct from demonstrated accuracy or broad authorization to automate adjudication.

kps.k: Governance proposals distribute responsibility across professionals, vendors and public institutions rather than treating disclaimers or blanket bans as sufficient.
kps.d: Discussing unresolved UPL allegations against OpenAI, McCormack favors deliberate policymaking over regulation driven by resource-dependent litigation and anticipates state variation in court–legislature authority. She questions limiting responsibility to frontier developers while excluding downstream legal-AI vendors. Gabe Pereyra identifies citations, traceable work and decomposition as influences on Harvey’s design; McCormack emphasizes auditable agent records. Practical recommendations include secure handling of nonpublic information, human verification and consent for recording. The hosts’ expectation that AI-specific restrictions may recede does not remove competence and confidentiality obligations, nor does their predicted future duty to use AI establish a current universal requirement.

kps.k: AI-assisted professional formation offers a possible alternative to lost routine training tasks, but its effects on independent judgment remain unresolved.
kps.d: Leonard and McCormack propose AI coaching, simulated audiences, conversational learning and competency-based training rather than prohibition or simple preservation of existing curricula. Dyane O’Leary reports classroom experimentation but rejects redesigning all legal education around generative AI. Daniel Schwarcz reports efficiency and increasingly evident quality gains in earlier comparative research, while identifying possible impairment of lawyers’ judgment and development as his leading concern; the supplied material does not provide the new study’s findings. Predictions of accelerated junior capability or returning generalists therefore remain hypotheses, not established substitutes for apprenticeship or specialist expertise.

kps.k: Service and business-model expansion is a forecast, not a demonstrated consequence of task automation.
kps.d: McCormack expects AAA’s excess workload to turn displaced tasks into greater capacity rather than fewer jobs. The hosts imagine agent-supported boutiques, subscription information services and lawyers concentrating on strategic client choices, while leaving junior employment prospects uncertain. Stephanie Wilkins distinguishes firms built around AI delivery from traditional firms with strong AI functions. Nikki Shaver describes an unresolved buyer choice between broad-platform offerings and specialist applications. These propositions concern different markets and should not be collapsed into a single prediction of employment growth, higher profits or vendor displacement.

kps.k: The practical research implication is to move from persuasive demonstrations and adoption counts to task-specific and legal-system outcome evidence.
kps.d: The cluster contains implementation accounts, personal experiments, reported surveys and attributed research, but little detailed outcome measurement. The Vals AI discussion describes independent vendor testing against a human baseline sourced through Cognia Law without supplying scores or rankings. McCormack and Leonard explicitly seek comparisons of access to legal information with and without AI. Such testing could distinguish use, satisfaction, work quality, independent learning and justice outcomes. Cross-sector medical and driving analogies motivate that agenda but do not validate legal applications. Episode titles, announced reports and AI-generated retrospectives likewise cannot supply findings absent from the excerpts.

vlens.an: The in-house counsel and legal-operations source frames generative AI as creating opportunities for innovation in the general counsel’s office, which is broadly compatible with the cluster’s practitioner-engagement agenda. However, the supplied excerpt is only Jen Leonard’s introduction and contains no substantive remarks from Ilona Logvinova or Darth Vaughn. It therefore does not establish whether these practitioners endorse experimentation before technological certainty, workflow redesign, shared implementation, human verification, governance, reliability safeguards or access-to-justice priorities. With no developed argument or evidence from the guests, neither a common rationale nor material internal variation within this professional voice can be assessed from this curated source.

The curated legal-tech-vendor sources do not provide enough substantive evidence to assign this professional voice a clear collective position on the cluster’s full proposition. John Nay supports its practitioner-experimentation component: he describes using AI to develop research hypotheses and sustain his involvement in legal-AI research. Gabe Pereyra’s account is compatible with iterative, human-directed use but chiefly identifies the practical difficulty of supplying context. This limitation reinforces the cluster’s view that useful adoption depends on inputs and implementation rather than software acquisition alone, without developing a legal-work redesign or governance prescription. Material internal variation is mainly evidentiary: the Barnwell excerpt ends before he makes substantive claims, while the Shaver excerpt redirects attention to product-selection complexity and the need for comparative market assessment. None of the supplied vendor excerpts substantively addresses the proposition’s wider concerns about reliability safeguards, shared responsibility, access to justice or judicial legitimacy. Thus, the available evidence leans toward experimentation but is too narrow and incomplete to establish overall support from this curated professional voice.

qs.q: We launched something recently called the Legal AGI Lab, and the only way that I can have time to get involved in that is to use AI to help with developing research hypotheses and thinking through ways to carry forward the work that we do there.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources generally accept the proposition’s case for learning through practical AI engagement, but they materially develop it by defining what responsible redesign should investigate and preserve. Hoffman and the legal-education discussion support bounded, human-directed experimentation: AI is used for research, comparison, reflection and teaching, while reported convenience and useful outputs are treated as anecdotal rather than proof of reliability. Schwarcz adds the strongest research extension, pairing reported efficiency and quality gains from earlier comparative work with an unresolved concern that AI may impair lawyers’ independent judgment and cognitive development. This turns the cluster’s caution into a concrete empirical agenda: redesign should assess work quality and professional formation, not adoption alone. Internal variation is material. O’Leary resists allowing generative AI to dominate the broader law-school curriculum, while Wilkins redirects attention toward AI-centred firms as an emerging service-delivery model rather than addressing practitioner engagement, reliability or shared implementation directly. Thus, these sources do not speak with one voice, and their number should not be read as indicating prevalence, but their principal contribution is to strengthen the proposition with pedagogical limits and task- and development-specific research questions.

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, courts and professional-body voices accepts the proposition’s core case for practitioner-led experimentation and materially develops it into an institutional programme for governed adoption. The recurring rationale is that courts, bar bodies and legal organisations should not wait for stable technology: they should build AI literacy, permit bounded trials, involve practising lawyers and affected users, and redesign workflows around concrete needs. At the same time, experimentation is generally framed as supervised rather than autonomous, with human review, confidentiality, consent, audit trails, task-specific risk controls and preservation of litigant voice and procedural fairness. Court-focused sources add distinctive concerns about public funding, training capacity, self-represented litigants and comparison against realistic alternatives such as fallible human decision-making or no legal help. Professional-body sources add nonbinding ethics guidance, competency frameworks and continuing education; governance-focused sources distribute responsibility among lawyers, vendors, model developers, courts and legislatures. Some sources go further by proposing comparative benchmarking and legal-system outcome research, which strengthens the proposition’s evidentiary discipline. Material internal variation concerns ambition and evidentiary confidence: some favour expansive redesign, direct public tools or AI-assisted adjudication, whereas others confine present use to low-risk assistance and high-stakes exclusions. Benefits for access to justice, capacity, careers and service quality remain mostly predictions or anecdotes, not demonstrated outcomes. A few excerpts are too introductory or off-topic to classify, but the supplied evidence contains no clear rejection of engagement; this should not be generalized beyond the curated sources.

Its support is cautious rather than evidentially conclusive: the reported judicial warmth is expressly not endorsement, and the excerpts provide no measured evidence on legal accuracy, economics, access-to-justice outcomes or comparative performance. Because the curated evidence contains only this source, it does not establish how common this position is among AI-native providers, and there is little basis for assessing internal variation within that professional voice.

vlens.an: Within this curated access-to-justice and civil-society voice, the sources support the proposition that practitioners should engage with and test AI now while preserving human responsibility, reliability and public-benefit concerns. Their common rationale is that AI may extend legal understanding and legal-aid capacity, and that practitioner involvement is necessary to determine useful applications and safeguards. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis: Cat Moon foregrounds practical, cautious experimentation and reports comparatively rapid legal-aid uptake; Angela Tripp proposes task-specific comparison with human error as a possible route to confidence; Afua Bruce and Jason Tashea stress that people design these systems and that present adoption should not be justified by speculative future benefits. This variation qualifies rather than reverses support. The evidence remains preliminary: reported uptake is not proof that unmet legal need has fallen, proposed human-performance comparisons are conditional, and the excerpts provide neither outcome data nor detailed implementation models.

vlens.an: This curated traditional-law-firm source supports the proposition that legal organisations should begin practitioner-led experimentation and workflow redesign without waiting for technological certainty. Its central rationale is implementation-focused: practising lawyers possess the context needed to identify useful applications, while innovation specialists should provide tools, instruction and brainstorming support rather than impose rigid workflows. The account also attributes adoption to leadership, broad access to tools and a culture that permits experimentation. Internal variation is mainly one of emphasis: Jen Reeves stresses practitioner autonomy and continued engagement; the hosts emphasise organisational culture and competitive advantage; practising lawyers report greater speed, creativity and enjoyment. These strands remain aligned rather than substantively divided. However, the claimed benefits are anecdotal or predictive, and unspecified engagement numbers do not establish reliability, legal-work quality or firm-wide performance gains. The source therefore supports experimentation and shared implementation, while also fitting the synthesis’s distinction between encouraging adoption experience and demonstrated outcomes. As a single curated account, it should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

vlens.an: Where these curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources directly address the proposition, they support practitioner engagement before technological certainty. The common rationale is that AI is best understood through routine experimentation—as a general-purpose aid for thinking, writing and other personal or professional tasks—and through adaptation of legal education and broader professional institutions rather than prohibition or passivity. The strongest source also calls for participation by law schools, firms, regulators, the judiciary and the public, aligning experimentation with shared responsibility for redesign. Material internal variation limits the breadth of this conclusion: Abramowitz relies on personal experience and predictions about diffuse benefits; the education-and-professional-dialogue source advances a broader reform agenda; Shaver chiefly forecasts future technology interfaces and offers selection advice; the power-rankings excerpt contains no substantive AI position; and the ChatGPT retrospective is the model’s synthesis rather than an endorsed source finding. These sources provide little direct treatment of verification, measured legal reliability or judicial legitimacy, while access-to-justice benefits appear mainly as an unsupported claim in an AI-generated retrospective. Thus, the professional voice supports the proposition’s engagement-and-redesign core, but does not independently substantiate its safeguards or claimed outcomes.

elens.an:
The 2023–2024 generative-shock sources collectively accept the proposition that legal practitioners should begin learning, experimenting and redesigning work before AI reaches technological certainty, and they materially develop it with early implementation models. The common rationale is that practical use builds literacy, reveals suitable workflows and allows legal professionals—rather than technology companies alone—to shape adoption. Concrete extensions include AAA’s beta-tested and fine-tuned Clause Builder AI, organisation-wide participation, baseline education, junior-lawyer involvement, professional-network learning, court–law-firm collaboration and accessible education for solo and small practices. The sources generally favour bounded assistance with human control rather than autonomous legal or judicial decision-making.

Material variation concerns setting and risk, not the core direction. Court-focused discussions stress public-funding and training disadvantages, litigants’ voices and judicial legitimacy; access-to-justice discussions emphasise legal understanding and extending legal aid’s reach; workplace accounts concentrate on drafting, training, communications and service design. Several sources expressly acknowledge hallucinations, AI washing, uneven capabilities and the need for safe deployment. Their optimism also varies from reports of an implemented tool to exploratory demonstrations, personal anecdotes and forecasts. Accordingly, these sources support redesign and experimentation more strongly than they establish reliability, productivity or improved justice outcomes. One corporate-legal-department excerpt is too limited to classify substantively, and none of the supplied sources clearly opposes the proposition. Because this is a curated set, this alignment should not be treated as representative of legal professionals generally or as evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: The Clause Builder AI tool—which went live a few weeks ago (we had it in beta for a while as we fine-tuned it)—is a version of our legacy Clause Builder tool.
qs.a: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal professionals should experiment with and redesign work around AI before the technology is fully settled, and they materially develop it through concrete implementation models. Common reasons include the speed of technological change; the risk that disengaged lawyers will cede design choices to technology companies or other outside entrants; the practical value users report from bounded assistance; and the possibility of redirecting lawyers toward strategic advice, human explanation and unmet legal need. The most substantive extensions are practitioner-designed workflows at Quinn Emanuel; AAA’s blank-slate case-management review and bounded AI-arbitrator initiatives; tool-agnostic change-management training; redesigned legal education and professional formation; supervised judicial uses; and task-specific benchmarking against human-lawyer baselines. Internal variation is material but does not reverse the overall direction. Some sources favour incremental pilots, while others advocate imagining large-scale redesign and working backwards. Access-to-justice sources prioritise direct public assistance and court capacity; education sources focus on competencies and apprenticeship; organisational sources emphasise leadership, integration and shared responsibility; and evaluation-focused sources call for comparative outcome data. Human involvement also ranges from augmentation and verification to more ambitious agentic services, although the concrete initiatives generally retain professional review and accountability. Tashea and Bruce add a sharper warning against adopting on the strength of developer promises, and other sources identify hallucinations, sycophancy, stale context, confidentiality, synthetic evidence and procedural legitimacy as constraints. These are qualifications to experimentation rather than arguments for waiting. The evidence base remains uneven: many benefits are anecdotes, forecasts or reported adoption signals, while deployments and training programmes establish activity rather than reliability, productivity, learning or access-to-justice outcomes. Two limited excerpts are unclear because they report use or an AI-generated retrospective without taking a sufficiently developed position.

qs.q: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.

qs.q: Each tool’s output was measured for accuracy, and VALS partnered with Cognia Law—an ALSP—to source human lawyers who also completed these tasks.

elens.an: The 2026 sources collectively accept the synthesis’s core case for practitioner engagement before technological certainty and materially develop how that approach should operate. The strongest contributions specify embedded implementation by lawyers and legal-operations professionals, business-context inputs, user education, human buy-in, auditable workflows, human oversight, differentiated disclosure, consent and risk-based limits for high-stakes uses. Schwarcz adds a distinct professional-formation concern: reported efficiency and quality gains do not resolve the possible impairment of lawyers’ independent judgment and development. Judicial-AI discussion extends the proposition through comparison with fallible human systems and unavailable legal help, while stopping short of demonstrated outcome benefits. Internal variation is material but not oppositional: several excerpts offer only personal workflows or predictions; others are too introductory to establish a position; and Wilkins redirects attention toward AI-centred firms as a distinct business model. Across this curated selection, claims about improved careers, agentic capabilities, market restructuring and access remain mainly experiential or prospective, whereas implementation and governance prescriptions are more concrete. The sources therefore strengthen the proposition operationally while reinforcing its call for task-specific evidence rather than treating adoption, satisfaction or launch activity as proof of reliability or legal-system benefit.
